entries.8093bc406bd65246080f8e0d63b22292aee416f8: <div sID="gen10389" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Ps.5" sID="Ps.5"/> <div eID="gen10389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10390" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10391" type="x-p"/> The psalm is a prayer, a solemn address to God, at a time when the psalmist was brought into distress by the malice of his enemies. Many such times passed over David, nay, there was scarcely any time of his life to which this psalm may not be accommodated, for in this he was a type of Christ, that he was continually beset with enemies, and his powerful and prevalent appeals to God, when he was so beset, pointed at Christ's dependence on his Father and triumphs over the powers of darkness in the midst of his sufferings. In this psalm, I. David settles a correspondence between his soul and God, promising to pray, and promising himself that God would certainly hear him, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1-Ps.5.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He gives to God the glory, and takes to himself the comfort, of God's holiness, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.4-Ps.5.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. III. He declares his resolution to keep close to the public worship of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">ver. 7</reference>. IV. He prayed, 1. For himself, that God would guide him,, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">ver. 8</reference>. 2. Against his enemies, that God would destroy them, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9-Ps.5.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. 3. For all the people of God, that God would give them joy, and keep them safe, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.11-Ps.5.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. And this is all of great use to direct us in prayer.
entries.21ce04c448a9a2273ebf9049962492209278509c: <div eID="gen10391" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10390" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for Guidance and Protection.</title> <div sID="gen10392" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Give ear to my words, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , consider my meditation. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hearken unto the voice of my cry, my King, and my God: for unto thee will I pray. <hi type="super">3</hi> My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; in the morning will I direct <hi type="italic">my prayer</hi> unto thee, and will look up. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness: neither shall evil dwell with thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> The foolish shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will abhor the bloody and deceitful man. <div eID="gen10392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10393" type="x-p"/> The title of this psalm has nothing in it peculiar but that it is said to be upon <hi type="italic">Nehiloth,</hi> a word nowhere else used. It is conjectured (and it is but a conjecture) that is signifies <hi type="italic">wind</hi>—instruments, with which this psalm was sung, as <hi type="italic">Neginoth</hi> was supposed to signify the <hi type="italic">stringed</hi>—instruments. In <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1-Ps.5.6">these verses</reference> David had an eye to God, <div eID="gen10393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10394" type="x-p"/> I. As a prayer-hearing God; such he has always been ever since men began to call upon the name of the Lord, and yet is still as ready to hear prayer as ever. Observe how David here styles him: <hi type="italic">O Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.3">3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> a self-existent, self-sufficient, Being, whom we are bound to adore, and, "<hi type="italic">my King and my God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.2">v. 2</reference>), whom I have avouched for my God, to whom I have sworn allegiance, and under whose protection I have put myself as my King." We believe that the God we pray to is a King, and a God. King of kings and God of gods; but that is not enough: the most commanding encouraging principle of prayer, and the most powerful or prevailing plea in prayer, is to look upon him as <hi type="italic">our</hi> King and <hi type="italic">our</hi> God, to whom we lie under peculiar obligations and from whom we have peculiar expectations. Now observe, <div eID="gen10394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10395" type="x-p"/> 1. What David here prays for, which may encourage our faith and hopes in all our addresses to God. If we pray fervently, and in faith, we have reason to hope, (1.) That God will take cognizance of our case, the representation we make of it and the requests we make upon it; for so he prays here: <hi type="italic">Give ear to my words, O Lord!</hi> Though God is in heaven, he has an ear open to his people's prayers, and it is not heavy, that he cannot hear. Men perhaps will not or cannot hear us; our enemies are so haughty that they will not, our friends at such a distance that they cannot; but God, though high, though in heaven, can, and will. (2.) That he will take it into his wise and compassionate consideration, and will not slight it, or turn it off with a cursory answer; for so he prays: <hi type="italic">Consider my meditation.</hi> David's prayers were not his words only, but his meditations; as meditation is the best preparative for prayer, so prayer is the best issue of meditation. Meditation and prayer should go together, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Ps. xix. 14</reference>. It is when we thus consider our prayers, and then only, that we may expect that God will consider them, and take that to his heart which comes from ours. (3.) That he will, in due time, return a gracious answer of peace; for so he prays (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hearken to the voice of my cry.</hi> His prayer was a <hi type="italic">cry;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">the voice of his cry,</hi> which denotes fervency of affection and importunity of expression; and such effectual fervent prayers of a righteous man avail much and do wonders. <div eID="gen10395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10396" type="x-p"/> 2. What David here promises, as the condition on his part to be performed, fulfilled, and kept, that he might obtain this gracious acceptance; this may guide and govern us in our addresses to God, that we may present them aright, for we ask, and have not, if we ask amiss. Four things David here promises, and so must we:—(1.) That he will pray, that he will make conscience of praying, and make a business of it: <hi type="italic">Unto thee will I pray.</hi> "Others live without prayer, but I will pray." Kings on their own thrones (so David was) must be beggars at God's throne. "Others pray to strange gods, and expect relief from them, but to thee, to thee only, will I pray." The assurances God has given us of his readiness to hear prayer should confirm our resolution to live and die praying. (2.) That he will pray <hi type="italic">in the morning.</hi> His praying voice shall be heard then, and then shall his prayer be directed; that shall be the date of his letters to heaven, not that only ("Morning, and evening, and at noon, will I pray, nay, seven times a day, will I praise thee"), but that certainly. Morning prayer is our duty; we are the fittest for prayer when we are in the most fresh, and lively, and composed frame, got clear of the slumbers of the night, revived by them, and not yet filled with the business of the day. We have then most need of prayer, considering the dangers and temptations of the day to which we are exposed, and against which we are concerned; by faith and prayer, to fetch in fresh supplies of grace. (3.) That he will have his eye single and his heart intent in the duty: <hi type="italic">I will direct my prayer,</hi> as a marksman directs his arrow to the white; with such a fixedness and steadiness of mind should we address ourselves to God. Or as we direct a letter to a friend at such a place so must we direct our prayers to God as our Father in heaven; and let us always send them by the Lord Jesus, the great Mediator, and then they will be sure not to miscarry. All our prayers must be directed to God; his honour and glory must be aimed at as our highest end in all our prayers. Let our first petition be, <hi type="italic">Hallowed,</hi> glorified, <hi type="italic">by thy name,</hi> and then we may be sure of the same gracious answer to it that was given to Christ himself: <hi type="italic">I have glorified it, and I will glorify it yet again.</hi> (4.) That he will patiently wait for an answer of peace: "I <hi type="italic">will look up,</hi> will look after my prayers, and <hi type="italic">hear what God the Lord will speak</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">Ps. lxxxv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab. ii. 1</reference>), that, if he grant what I asked, I may be thankful—if he deny, I may be patient—if he defer, I may continue to pray and wait and may not faint." We must look <hi type="italic">up,</hi> or look <hi type="italic">out,</hi> as he that has shot an arrow looks to see how near it has come to the mark. We lose much of the comfort of our prayers for want of observing the returns of them. Thus praying, thus waiting, as the lame man looked stedfastly on Peter and John (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.4">Acts iii. 4</reference>), we may expect that God will give ear to our words and consider them, and to him we may refer ourselves, as David here, who does not pray, "Lord, do this, or the other, for me;" but, "Hearken to me, consider my case, and do in it as seemeth good unto thee." <div eID="gen10396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10397" type="x-p"/> II. As a sin-hating God, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.4-Ps.5.6">v. 4-6</reference>. David takes notice of this, 1. As a warning to himself, and all other praying people, to remember that, as the God with whom we have to do is gracious and merciful, so he is pure and holy; though he is ready to hear prayer, yet, if we regard iniquity in our heart, he /ill not hear our prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Ps. lxvi. 18</reference>. 2. As an encouragement to his prayers against his enemies; they were wicked men, and therefore enemies to God, and such as he had not pleasure in. See here. (1.) The holiness of God's nature. When he says, <hi type="italic">Thou art not a God that has pleasure in wickedness,</hi> he means, "Thou art a God that hates it, as directly contrary to thy infinite purity and rectitude, and holy will." Though the workers of iniquity prosper, let none thence infer that God has pleasure in wickedness, no, not in that by which men pretend to honour him, as those do that hate their brethren, and cast them out, and say, <hi type="italic">Let the Lord be glorified.</hi> God has no pleasure in wickedness, though covered with a cloak of religion. Let those therefore who delight in sin know that God has no delight in them; nor let any say, when he is tempted, <hi type="italic">I am tempted of God,</hi> for God is not the author of sin, neither <hi type="italic">shall evil dwell with him,</hi> that is, it shall not always be countenanced and suffered to prosper. Dr. Hammond thinks this refers to that law of Moses which would not permit strangers, who persisted in their idolatry, to dwell in the land of Israel. (2.) The justice of his government. The foolish <hi type="italic">shall not stand in his sight,</hi> that is, shall not be smiled upon by him, nor admitted to attend upon him, nor shall they be acquitted in the judgment of the great day. The workers of iniquity are very foolish. Sin is folly, and sinners are the greatest of all fools; not fools of God's making (those are to be pitied), for he hates nothing that he has made, but fools of their own making, and those he hates. Wicked people hate God; justly therefore are they hated of him, and it will be their endless misery and ruin. "Those whom thou hatest thou shalt destroy;" particularly two sorts of sinners, who are here marked for destruction:—[1.] Those that are fools, that speak leasing or lying, and that are deceitful. There is a particular emphasis laid on these sinners (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.8">Rev. xxi. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">All liars,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.15">Ps. xxii. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whosoever loves and makes a lie;</hi> nothing is more contrary than this, and therefore nothing more hateful to the God of truth. [2.] Those that are cruel: <hi type="italic">Thou wilt abhor the bloody man;</hi> for inhumanity is no less contrary, no less hateful, to the God of mercy, whom mercy pleases. Liars and murderers are in a particular manner said to resemble the devil and to be his children, and therefore it may well be expected that God should abhor them. These were the characters of David's enemies; and such as these are still the enemies of Christ and his church, men perfectly lost to all virtue and honour; and the worse they are the surer we may be of their ruin in due time. <div eID="gen10397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10398" type="x-p"/> In singing <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1-Ps.5.6">these verses</reference>, and praying them over, we must engage and stir up ourselves to the duty of prayer, and encourage ourselves in it, because we shall not seek the Lord in vain; and must express our detestation of sin, and our awful expectation of that day of Christ's appearing which will be the day of the perdition of ungodly men.
entries.4a99ac096900d87fd896ad3a72481118f004afd4: <div eID="gen10398" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Delight in Public Worship; Happiness of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen10399" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> But as for me, I will come <hi type="italic">into</hi> thy house in the multitude of thy mercy: <hi type="italic">and</hi> in thy fear will I worship toward thy holy temple. <hi type="super">8</hi> Lead me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , in thy righteousness because of mine enemies; make thy way straight before my face. <hi type="super">9</hi> For <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no faithfulness in their mouth; their inward part <hi type="italic">is</hi> very wickedness; their throat <hi type="italic">is</hi> an open sepulchre; they flatter with their tongue. <hi type="super">10</hi> Destroy thou them, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; cast them out in the multitude of their transgressions; for they have rebelled against thee. <hi type="super">11</hi> But let all those that put their trust in thee rejoice: let them ever shout for joy, because thou defendest them: let them also that love thy name be joyful in thee. <hi type="super">12</hi> For thou, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as <hi type="italic">with</hi> a shield. <div eID="gen10399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10400" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.7">these verses</reference> David gives three characters—of himself, of his enemies, and of all the people of God, and subjoins a prayer to each of them. <div eID="gen10400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10401" type="x-p"/> I. He gives an account of himself and prays for himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7-Ps.5.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen10401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10402" type="x-p"/> 1. He is stedfastly resolved to keep closely to God and to his worship. Sinners go away from God, and so make themselves odious to his holiness and obnoxious to his justice: "<hi type="italic">But, as for me,</hi> that shall not keep me from thee." God's holiness and justice are so far from being a terror to the upright in heart, to drive them from God, that they are rather by them invited to cleave to him. David resolves, (1.) To worship God, to pay his homage to him, and give unto God the glory due unto his name. (2.) To worship him publicly: "<hi type="italic">I will come into thy house,</hi> the courts of thy house, to worship there with other faithful worshippers." David was much in secret worship, prayed often alone (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.2-Ps.5.3">v. 2, 3</reference>), and yet was very constant and devout in his attendance on the sanctuary. The duties of the closet are designed to prepare us for, not to excuse us from, public ordinances. (3.) To worship him reverently and with a due sense of the infinite distance there is between God and man: "<hi type="italic">In thy fear will I worship,</hi> with a holy awe of God upon my spirit," <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">Heb. xii. 28</reference>. God is greatly to be feared by all his worshippers. (4.) To take his encouragement, in worship, from God himself only. [1.] From his infinite mercy. It is in the multitude of God's mercy (the inexhaustible treasures of mercy that are in God and the innumerable proofs and instances of it which we receive from him) that David confides, and not in any merit or righteousness of his own, in his approaches to God. The mercy of God should ever be both the foundation of our hopes and the fountain of our joy in every thing wherein we have to do with him. [2.] From the instituted medium of worship, which was then the temple, here called <hi type="italic">the temple of his holiness,</hi> as a type of Christ, the great and only Mediator, who sanctifies the service as the temple sanctified the gold, and to whom we must have an eye in all our devotions as the worshippers then had to the temple. <div eID="gen10402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10403" type="x-p"/> 2. He earnestly prays that God, by his grace, would guide and preserve him always in the way of his duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lead me in thy righteousness, because of my enemies</hi>—Heb. "<hi type="italic">Because of those who observe me,</hi> who watch for my halting and seek occasion against me." See here, (1.) The good use which David made of the malice of his enemies against him. The more curious they were in spying faults in him, that they might have whereof to accuse him, the more cautious he was to avoid sin and all appearances of it, and the more solicitous to be always found in the good way of God and duty. Thus, by wisdom and grace, good may come out of evil. (2.) The right course which David took for the baffling of those who sought occasion against him. He committed himself to a divine guidance, begged of God both by his providence and by his grace to direct him in the right way, and keep him from turning aside out of it, at any time, in any instance whatsoever, that the most critical and captious of his enemies, like Daniel's, might find no occasion against him. The way of our duty is here called <hi type="italic">God's way,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his righteousness,</hi> because he prescribes to us by his just and holy laws, which if we sincerely set before us as our rule, we may in faith beg of God to direct us in all particular cases. How this prayer of David's was answered to him see <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.14-1Sam.18.15">1 Sam. xviii. 14, 15</reference>. <div eID="gen10403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10404" type="x-p"/> II. He gives an account of his enemies, and prays against them, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9-Ps.5.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. 1. If his account of them is true, as no doubt it is, they have a very bad character; and, if they had not been bad men indeed, they could not have been enemies to a man after God's own heart. He had spoken (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.6">v. 6</reference>) of God's hating the bloody and deceitful man. "Now, Lord," says he, "that is the character of my enemies: they are deceitful; there is no trusting them, for there is no faithfulness in their mouth." They thought it was no sin to tell a deliberate lie if it might but blemish David, and render him odious. "<hi type="italic">Lord, lead me,</hi>" says he (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">v. 8</reference>), "for such as these are the men I have to do with, against whose slanders innocency itself is no security. Do they speak fair? Do they talk of peace and friendship? <hi type="italic">They flatter with their tongues;</hi> it is designed to cover their malice, and to gain their point the more securely. Whatever they pretend of religion or friendship, two sacred things, they are true to neither: <hi type="italic">Their inward part is wickedness</hi> itself; it is <hi type="italic">very wickedness.</hi> They are likewise bloody; for <hi type="italic">their throat is an open sepulchre,</hi> cruel as the grave, gaping to devour and to swallow up, insatiable as the grave, which never says, <hi type="italic">It is enough,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15-Prov.30.16">Prov. xxx. 15, 16</reference>. This is quoted (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.13">Rom. iii. 13</reference>) to show the general corruption of mankind; for they are all naturally prone to malice, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.3">Tit. iii. 3</reference>. The grave is opened for them all, and yet they are as open graves to one another. 2. If his prayer against them is heard, as no doubt it is, they are in a bad condition. As men are, and do, so they must expect to fare. He prays to God to destroy them (according to what he had said <reference osisRef="Ps.5.6">v. 6</reference>, "Thou shalt destroy men of this character," so <hi type="italic">let them fall;</hi> and sinners would soon throw themselves into ruin if they were let alone), to <hi type="italic">cast them out</hi> of his protection and favour, out of the heritage of the Lord, out of the land of the living; and woe to those whom God casts out. "They have by their sins deserved destruction; there is enough to justify God in their utter rejection: <hi type="italic">Cast them out in the multitude of their transgressions,</hi> by which they have filled up the measure of their iniquity and have become ripe for ruin." Persecuting God's servants fills the measure as soon as any thing, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1 Thess. ii. 15, 16</reference>. Nay, they may be easily made to <hi type="italic">fall by their own counsels;</hi> that which they do to secure themselves, and do mischief to others, by the over-ruling providence of God may be made a means of their destruction, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15">Ps. vii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.15">ix. 15</reference>. He pleads, "<hi type="italic">They have rebelled against thee.</hi> Had they been only my enemies, I could safely have forgiven them; but they are rebels against God, his crown and dignity; they oppose his government, and will not repent, to give him glory, and therefore I plainly foresee their ruin." His prayer for their destruction comes not from a spirit of revenge, but from a spirit of prophecy, by which he foretold that all who rebel against God will certainly be destroyed by their own counsels. If it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to those that trouble his people, as we are told it is (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6">2 Thess. i. 6</reference>), we pray that it may be done whenever we pray, <hi type="italic">Father, thy will be done.</hi> <div eID="gen10404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10405" type="x-p"/> III. He gives an account of the people of God, and prays for them, concluding with an assurance of their bliss, which he doubted not of his own interest in. Observe, 1. The description he gives of God's people. They are the righteous (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.12">v. 12</reference>); for they <hi type="italic">put their trust in God,</hi> are well assured of his power and all-sufficiency, venture their all upon his promise, and are confident of his protection in the way of their duty; and they <hi type="italic">love his name,</hi> are well pleased with all that by which God has made himself known, and take delight in their acquaintance with him. This is true and pure religion, to live a life of complacency in God and dependence on him. 2. His prayer for them: "<hi type="italic">Let them rejoice;</hi> let them have cause to rejoice and hearts to rejoice; fill them with joy, with great joy and unspeakable; let them shout for joy, with constant joy and perpetual; <hi type="italic">let them ever shout for joy,</hi> with holy joy, and that which terminates in God; <hi type="italic">let them be joyful in thee,</hi> in thy favour, in thy salvation, not in any creature. Let them rejoice <hi type="italic">because thou defendest them,</hi> coverest them, or overshadowest them, dwellest among them." Perhaps here is an allusion to the pillar of cloud and fire, which was to Israel a visible token of God's special presence with them and the special protection they were under. Let us learn of David to pray, not for ourselves only, but for others, for all good people, for all that trust in God and love his name, though not in every thing of our mind nor in our interest. Let all that are entitled to God's promises have a share in our prayers; grace be with all that love Christ in sincerity. This is to concur with God. 3. His comfort concerning them, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.12">v. 12</reference>. He takes them into his prayers because they are God's peculiar people; therefore he doubts not but his prayers shall be heard, and they shall always rejoice; for, (1.) They are happy in the assurance of God's blessing: "<hi type="italic">Thou, Lord, wilt bless the righteous,</hi> wilt command a blessing upon them. Thou hast in thy word pronounced them blessed, and therefore wilt make them truly so. <hi type="italic">Those whom thou blessest are blessed indeed.</hi>" (2.) "They are safe under the protection of thy favour; with that thou wilt <hi type="italic">crown</hi> him" (so some read it); "it is his honour, will be to him a diadem of beauty, and make him truly great: with that thou <hi type="italic">wilt compass him,</hi> wilt surround him, on every side, <hi type="italic">as with a shield.</hi>" A shield, in war, guards only one side, but the favour of God is to the saints a defence on every side; like the hedge about Job, round about, so that, while they keep themselves under the divine protection, they are entirely safe and ought to be entirely satisfied. <div eID="gen10405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10406" type="x-p"/> In singing <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7-Ps.5.12">these verses</reference>, and praying them over, we must by faith put ourselves under God's guidance and care, and then please ourselves with his mercy and grace and with the prospect of God's triumphs at last over all his enemies and his people's triumphs in him and in his salvation.  <chapter eID="Ps.5"/> <div eID="gen10406" type="x-p"/>

entries.8f70d7294699f17cbb3fbe97f9fc0155c414a479: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5488"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.5.1-Ps.5.12">Psa 5:1-12</reference>. Upon Nehiloth--flutes or wind instruments. The writer begs to be heard, on the ground of God's regard for His covenant-people and true worshippers as contrasted with His holy hatred to the wicked. He prays for divine guidance, on account of his watchful, malignant, and deceitful enemies; and for their destruction as being also God's enemies. At the same time he expresses his confidence that God will extend aid to His people.</title> <div sID="gen8316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5488"/><hi type="bold">1. meditation--</hi>moanings of that half-uttered form to which deep feeling gives rise--groanings, as in <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.27">27</reference>. <div eID="gen8316" type="x-p"/>

entries.92a689711f58188a81ccd3e0a24a0576de3dc2b2: <div eID="gen18409" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18410" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18411" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18411" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18410" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18412" type="x-p"/> David continues instant in prayers <reference osisRef="Psa.5.1">Psa 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.2">Psa 5:2</reference>; makes early application to God, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.3">Psa 5:3</reference>; and shows the hatred which God bears to the workers of iniquity, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.4-Psa.5.6">Psa 5:4-6</reference>. His determination to worship God, and to implore direction and support, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.7">Psa 5:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>. He points out the wickedness of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>, and the destruction they may expect, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.10">Psa 5:10</reference>; and then shows the happiness of those who trust in the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.5.12">Psa 5:12</reference>. <div eID="gen18412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18413" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is inscribed to the chief Musician upon Nehiloth, A Psalm of David. As neginoth may signify all kinds of instruments struck with a plectrum, stringed instruments, those like the drum, cymbals, etc.; so nechiloth, from חל chal, to be hollow, to bore through, may signify any kind of wind instruments, such as the horn, trumpet, flute, etc. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.4.1-Psa.4.8">Psa 4:1-8</reference> (note). The Septuagint have, Εις το τελος, ὑπερ της κληρονομουσης, "In favor of her who obtains the inheritance." The Vulgate and Arabic have a similar reading. The word נחילות nechiloth they have derived from נחל nachal, to inherit. This may either refer to the Israelites who obtained the inheritance of the promised land, or to the Church of Christ which obtains through him, by faith and prayer, the inheritance among the saints in light. This Psalm is, especially, for the whole Church of God. <div eID="gen18413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18414" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18415" type="x-p"/> Give ear to my words - This is properly a morning hymn, as the preceding was an evening hymn. We have seen from the conclusion of the last Psalm that David was very happy, and lay down and slept in the peace and love of his God. When he opens his eyes on the following morning, he not only remembers but feels the happiness of which he spoke; and with his first recollections he meditates on the goodness and mercy of God, and the glorious state of salvation into which he had been brought. He calls on God to give ear to his words; probably words of God's promises which he had been pleading.
entries.d1394758f5ea0fcaec5d42043468225b76454590: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18416" type="x-p"/> Hearken unto the voice of my cry - We may easily find the process through which David's mind was now passing: <div eID="gen18416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18417" type="x-p"/> 1. We have seen from the preceding Psalm that he lay down in a very happy frame of mind, and that he had enjoyed profound repose. <div eID="gen18417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18418" type="x-p"/> 2. As soon as he awakes in the morning, his heart, having a right direction, resumes its work. <div eID="gen18418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18419" type="x-p"/> 3. He meditates on God's goodness; and on his own happy state, though pursued by enemies, and only safe as long as God preserved him by an almighty hand and especial providence. <div eID="gen18419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18420" type="x-p"/> 4. This shows him the need he has of the continual protection of the Most High; and therefore he begins to form his meditation and the desires of his heart into words, to which he entreats the Lord to give ear. <div eID="gen18420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18421" type="x-p"/> 5. As he was accustomed to have answers to his prayers, he feels the necessity of being importunate! and therefore lifts up his voice. <div eID="gen18421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18422" type="x-p"/> 6. Seeing the workers of iniquity, liars, and blood-thirsty men strong to accomplish their own purposes in the destruction of the godly, he becomes greatly in earnest, and cries unto the Lord: "Hearken unto the voice of my cry." <div eID="gen18422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18423" type="x-p"/> 7. He knows that, in order to have a right answer, he must have a proper disposition of mind. He feels his subjection to the supreme authority of the Most High, and is ready to do his will and obey his laws; therefore he prays to God as his lying: "Hearken, my King and my God." I have not only taken thee for my God, to save, defend, and make me happy; but I have taken thee for my King, to govern, direct, and rule over me. <div eID="gen18423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18424" type="x-p"/> 8. Knowing the necessity and success of prayer, he purposes to continue in the spirit and practice of it: "Unto thee will I pray." R. S. Jarchi gives this a pretty and pious turn: "When I have power to pray, and to ask for the things I need, then, O Lord, give ear to my words; but when I have no power to plead with thee, and fear seizes on my heart, then, O Lord, consider my meditation!"
entries.b5e76ef60a6be9182ba14aca2571daeb19c2050f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18425" type="x-p"/> My voice shalt thou hear in the morning - We find from this that he had not prayed in vain. He had received a blessed answer; God had lifted upon him the light of his countenance, and he therefore determines to be an early applicant at the throne of grace: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning." He finds it good to begin the day with God; to let Divine things occupy the first place in his waking thoughts; as that which first occupies the mind on awaking is most likely to keep possession of the heart all the day through. <div eID="gen18425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18426" type="x-p"/> In the morning will I direct my prayer - Here seems to be a metaphor taken from an archer. He sees his mark; puts his arrow in his bow; directs his shaft to the mark, i.e., takes his aim; lets fly, and then looks up, to see if he have hit his mark. Prayers that have a right aim, will have a prompt answer; and he who sends up his petitions to God through Christ, from a warm, affectionate heart, may confidently look up for an answer, for it will come. If an immediate answer be not given, let not the upright heart suppose that the prayer is not heard. It has found its way to the throne; and there it is registered.
entries.ede18c14c9b401d5d45bdffa803aa889eb32bf67: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18427" type="x-p"/> Neither shall evil dwell with thee - As thou art holy, so thou hast pleasure only in holiness; and as to evil men, they shall never enter into thy glory; לא יגרך רע lo yegurecha ra, "the evil man shall not even sojourn with thee."
entries.2f1fb43ba04204d7652280869a5dca26f95e5055: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18428" type="x-p"/> The foolish shall not stand - He is a fool and a madman who is running himself out of breath for no prize, who is fighting against the Almighty; this every wicked man does; therefore is every wicked man a fool and a madman. <div eID="gen18428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18429" type="x-p"/> Thou hatest all workers of iniquity - Some sin now and then, others generally; some constantly, and some labor in it with all their might. These are the Workers of iniquity. Such even the God of infinite love and mercy hates. Alas! what a portion have the workers of iniquity! the hatred of God Almighty!
entries.6f8a454ab92ff439ed464e68ef30aec162459fa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18430" type="x-p"/> That speak leasing - Falsity, from the Anglo-Saxon leasunge, a lie, falsity, deceit; from leas, lie, which is from the verb leasian to lie. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.4.2">Psa 4:2</reference> (note). <div eID="gen18430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18431" type="x-p"/> The Lord will abhor the bloody and deceitful man - איש דמים ish damim, the man of bloods; for he who has the spirit of a murderer, will rarely end with one bloodshedding. So the Jews, who clamored for the blood of our Lord, added to that, as far and as long as they could, the blood of his disciples.
entries.5df27406afd095c9655b78870d34214658bfe805: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18432" type="x-p"/> In the multitude of thy mercy - David considered it an inexpressible privilege to be permitted to attend public worship; and he knew that it was only through the multitude of God's mercy that he, or any man else, could enjoy such a privilege. He knew farther that, from the multitude of this mercy, he might receive innumerable blessings in his house. In this spirit, and with this dependence, he went to the house of the Lord. He who takes David's views of this subject will never, willingly, be absent from the means of grace. <div eID="gen18432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18433" type="x-p"/> In thy fear - Duly considering the infinite holiness of thy majesty, will I worship, אשתחוה eshtachaveh, will I bow and prostrate myself in the deepest self-abasement and humility. <div eID="gen18433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18434" type="x-p"/> Toward thy holy temple - If David was the author of this Psalm, as is generally agreed, the temple was not built at this time: only the tabernacle then existed; and in the preceding clause he speaks of coming into the house, by which he must mean the tabernacle. But temple here may signify the holy of holies, before which David might prostrate himself while in the house, i.e., the court of the tabernacle. Even in the house of God, there is the temple of God; the place where the Divine Shechinah dwells. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. In him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. In all ages and dispensations, Jesus was ever the temple where the Supreme Deity was met with and worshipped. The human nature of Jesus was the real temple of the Deity. Nowhere else can God be found.
entries.03305d717146e620b769a34c5108108590331084: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18435" type="x-p"/> Lead me, O Lord, in thy righteousness - When entered into the house, and prostrated before the temple, he knew that, unless God continued to lead and direct, he was not likely to profit even by such great advantages. We need God not only to bring us to his house, but to keep our feet while we are there. <div eID="gen18435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18436" type="x-p"/> Because of mine enemies - His conduct was marked; his enemies looked upon and watched him with an evil eye. They would have been glad of his halting, that they might have brought a reproach on the good cause which he had espoused. O how cautiously should those walk who make a profession of living to God, of knowing themselves to be in his favor, and of being delivered from all sin in this life! <div eID="gen18436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18437" type="x-p"/> Make thy way straight - Show me that I must go right on; and let thy light always shine on my path, that I may see how to proceed.
entries.ab2d65a2058be2a97932c99bd7eae4a6d11c9e52: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18438" type="x-p"/> No faithfulness in their mouth - They make professions of friendship; but all is hollow and deceitful: "They flatter with their tongue." <div eID="gen18438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18439" type="x-p"/> Very wickedness - Their heart is full of all kinds of depravity. <div eID="gen18439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18440" type="x-p"/> Their throat is an open sepulcher - It is continually gaping for the dead; and sends forth effluvia destructive to the living. I fear that this is too true a picture of the whole human race, totally corrupt within, and abominable without. The heart is the center and spring of this corruption; and the words and actions of men, which proceed from this source, will send out incessant streams of various impurity; and thus they continue till the grace of God changes and purifies the heart.
entries.88a22b1c90914aa972167176f827a30e3dedf919: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18441" type="x-p"/> Destroy thou them, O God - All these apparently imprecatory declarations should be translated in the future tense, to which they belong; and which shows them to be prophetic. Thou Wilt destroy them; thou Wilt cast them out, etc.
entries.07b95e0c35c24387f5244d1840bb8168159904d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen18441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18442" type="x-p"/> Let all those that put their trust in thee rejoice - Such expressions as these should be translated in the same way, declaratively and prophetically: "All those who put their trust in thee Shall rejoice, - Shall ever shout for joy."
entries.422d7a7b56c2cf54ba8a1d039491669a3234098f: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen18442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18443" type="x-p"/> For thou, Lord, wilt bless the righteous - A righteous soul is a peculiar object of God's affectionate regards; and therefore will be a subject of continual blessing. <div eID="gen18443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18444" type="x-p"/> With favor - Literally, Like a shield, thy favor will crown him. God loves such; and this love is their defense. In all places, times and circumstances, it will preserve them. "Keep yourselves," says the apostle, "in the love of God." He who abides in this love need not fear the face of any adversary. Thus ended the morning's devotion of this excellent man: a model by which every Christian may frame his own.  <chapter eID="Ps.5"/> <div eID="gen18444" type="x-p"/>

entries.d474d17c7fdbe30ceccb9533535e1cdce3349879: <div eID="gen9071" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Morning Prayer before Going to the House of God</title> <div sID="gen9072" type="x-p"/> The evening prayer is now followed by a second morning prayer, which like the former draws to a close with כּי־אתּה (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.8">Psa 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.5.12">Psa 5:12</reference>). The situation is different from that in <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1">Psa 3:1</reference>-8. In that Psalm David is fleeing, here he is in Jerusalem and anticipates going up to the Temple service. If this Psalm also belongs to the time of the rebellion of Absolom, it must have been written when the fire which afterwards broke forth was already smouldering in secret. <div eID="gen9072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9073" type="x-p"/> The inscription אל־הנּחילות is certainly not a motto indicative of its contents (lxx, Vulg., Luther, Hengstenberg). As such it would stand after מזמור. Whatever is connected with למנצח, always has reference to the music. If נחילות came from נחל it might according to the biblical use of this verb signify “inheritances,” or according to its use in the Talmud “swarms,” and in fact swarms of bees (Arab. <hi type="italic">naḥl</hi>); and נחילות ought then to be the beginning of a popular melody to which the Psalm is adapted. Hai Gaon understands it to denote a melody resembling the hum of bees; Reggio a song that sings of bees. Or is נחילות equivalent to נחלּות (<hi type="italic">excavatae</hi>) and this a special name for the flutes (חלילים)? The use of the flute in the service of the sanctuary is attested by <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sa 10:5</reference>; 1Ki 1:40.<note placement="foot">On the use of the flute in the second Temple, vid., Introduction p. 19.</note> <div eID="gen9073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9074" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">praep</hi>. אל was, then, more appropriate than על; because, as Redslob has observed, the singer cannot play the flute at the same time, but can only sing to the playing of another. <div eID="gen9074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9075" type="x-p"/> The Psalm consists of four six line strophes. The lines of the strophes here and there approximate to the caesura-schema. They consist of a rising and a sudden lowering. The German language, which uses so many more words, is not adapted to this caesura-schema [and the same may be said of the English].
entries.bba5b46dd99e28e1d293c2b8b5bf9c6a522e94d1: <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1-Ps.5.3">Psa 5:1-3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_5:2-4) <hi type="italic">The introit</hi>: Prayer to be heard. The thoughts are simple but the language is carefully chosen. אמרים is the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. of אמר (אמר), one of the words peculiar to the poetic prophetical style. The denominative האזין (like <hi type="italic">audire</hi> = <hi type="italic">aus</hi>, οὖς <hi type="italic">dare</hi>) belongs more to poetry than prose. הגיג (like אביב) or מחיר (like מחיר) occurs only in two Psalms לדוד, viz., here and Psa 34:4. It is derived from הגג = הגה (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Psa 1:2</reference>) and signifies that which is spoken meditatively, here praying in rapt devotion. Beginning thus the prayer gradually rises to a <hi type="italic">vox clamoris</hi>. שׁועי from שׁוע, to be distinguished from שׁוּעי (inf. Pi.) <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>, is one word with the Aram. צוח, Aethiop. צוּע (to call). On הקשׁיב used of intent listening, vid., Psa 10:17. The invocation מלכּי ואלהי, when it is a king who utters it, is all the more significant. David, and in general the theocratic king, is only the representative of the Invisible One, whom he with all Israel adores as his King. Prayer to Him is his first work as he begins the day. In the morning, בּקר (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.8">Psa 65:8</reference> for בּבּקר, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.13">Psa 88:13</reference>), shalt Thou hear my cry, is equivalent to my cry which goes forth with the early morn. Hupfeld considers the mention of the morning as only a “poetical expression” and when getting rid of the meaning <hi type="italic">prima luce</hi>, he also gets rid of the beautiful and obvious reference to the daily sacrifice. The verb ערך is the word used of laying the wood in order for the sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.7">Lev 1:7</reference>, and the pieces of the sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.8">Lev 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.12">Lev 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.6.5">Lev 6:5</reference>, of putting the sacred lamps in order, <reference osisRef="Exod.27.21">Exo 27:21</reference>; Lev 24:3., and of setting the shew-bread in order, <reference osisRef="Exod.40.23">Exo 40:23</reference>; Lev 24:8. The laying of the wood in order for the morning offering of a lamb (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.5">Lev 6:5</reference> [Lev 6:12], cf. Num 28:4) was one of the first duties of the priest, as soon as the day began to dawn; the lamb was slain before sun-rise and when the sun appeared above the horizon laid piece by piece upon the altar. The morning prayer is compared to this morning sacrifice. This is in its way also a sacrifice. The object which David has in his mind in connection with אערך is תּפלּתי. As the priests, with the early morning, lay the wood and pieces of the sacrifices of the <hi type="italic">Tamı̂d</hi> upon the altar, so he brings his prayer before God as a spiritual sacrifice and looks out for an answer (צפּה <hi type="italic">speculari</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab 2:1</reference>), perhaps as the priest looks out for fire from heaven to consume the sacrifice, or looks to the smoke to see that it rises up straight towards heaven.
entries.bb30ec4ddc32d6a9e0de9b35404b7caa9cd01b4f: <reference osisRef="Ps.5.4-Ps.5.6">Psa 5:4-6</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_5:5-7) The basing of the prayer on God’s holiness. The verbal adjective חפץ (coming from the primitive signification of adhering firmly which is still preserved in Arab. <hi type="italic">chfd, fut. i</hi>.) is in the <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. always (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.13">Psa 34:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.27">Psa 35:27</reference>) joined with the accusative. רע is conceived as a person, for although גּוּר may have a material object, it cannot well have a material subject. יגרך is used for brevity of expression instead of יגוּר עמּך (Ges. §121, 4). The verb גּוּר (to turn in, to take up one’s abode with or near any one) frequently has an accusative object, <reference osisRef="Ps.120.5">Psa 120:5</reference>, Jdg 5:17, and <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa 33:14</reference> according to which the light of the divine holiness is to sinners a consuming fire, which they cannot endure. Now there follow specific designations of the wicked. הוללים <hi type="italic">part</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal = hōlalim</hi>, or even <hi type="italic">Poal = hôlalim</hi> (= מהוללים),<note placement="foot">On the rule, according to which here, as in שׁוררי <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference> and the like, a simple <hi type="italic">Shebâ mobile</hi> goes over into <hi type="italic">Chateph pathach</hi> with <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> preceding it, vid., the observations on giving a faithful representation of the O.T. text according to the Masora in the <hi type="italic">Luther Zeitschr</hi>. 1863. S. 411. The Babylonian Ben-Naphtali (about 940) prefers the simple <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi> in such cases, as also in others; Ben-Asher of the school of Tiberias, whom the Masora follows, and whom consequently our Masoretic text ought to follow, prefers the <hi type="italic">Chateph</hi>, vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi> ii. 460-467.</note> are the foolish, and more especially foolish boasters; the primary notion of the verb is not that of being hollow, but that of sounding, then of loud boisterous, non-sensical behaviour. Of such it is said, that they are not able to maintain their position when they become manifest before the eye of God (לנגד as in <reference osisRef="Ps.101.7">Psa 101:7</reference> manifest before any one, from נגד to come forward, be visible far off, be distinctly visible). פעלי און are those who work (οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Mat 7:23</reference>) iniquity; און breath (ἄνεμος) is sometimes trouble, in connection with which one pants, sometimes wickedness, in which there is not even a trace of any thing noble, true, or pure. Such men Jahve hates; for if He did not hate evil (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.5">Psa 11:5</reference>), His love would not be a holy love. In דּברי כזב, דּברי is the usual form in combination when the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. is used, instead of מדבּרי. It is the same in Psa 58:4. The style of expression is also Davidic in other respects, viz., אישׁ דּמים וּמרמה as in Ps 55:24, and אבּד as in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.6">Psa 9:6</reference>, cf. Psa 21:11. תּעב (in Amos, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference> תּאב) appears to be a secondary formation from עוּב, like תּאב to desire, from אבה, and therefore to be of a cognate root with the Aram. עיּב to despise, treat with indignity, and the Arabic <hi type="italic">‛aib</hi> a stain (cf. on <reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">Lam 2:1</reference>). The fact that, as Hengstenberg has observed, wickedness and the wicked are described in a sevenfold manner is perhaps merely accidental.
entries.582c5ec9f7817a57dc341993506e26041e6b4afa: <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7-Ps.5.9">Psa 5:7-9</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_5:8-10) Since the Psalm is a morning hymn, the <hi type="italic">futt</hi>. in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference> state what he, on the contrary, may and will do (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.13">Psa 66:13</reference>). By the greatness and fulness of divine favour (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.14">Psa 116:14</reference>) he has access (εἴσοδον, for בּוא means, according to its root, “to enter”) to the sanctuary, and he will accordingly repair thither to-day. It is the tabernacle on Zion in which was the ark of the covenant that is meant here. That daily liturgical service was celebrated there must be assumed, since the ark of the covenant is the sign and pledge of Jahve’s presence; and it is, moreover, attested by 1Ch 16:37. It is also to be supposed that sacrifice was offered daily before the tabernacle. For it is not to be inferred from 1Ch 16:39. that sacrifice was only offered regularly on the <hi type="italic">Bama</hi> (high place) in Gibeon before the Mosaic tabernacle.<note placement="foot">Thus, in particular, Stähelin, <hi type="italic">Zur Kritik der Psalmen</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitschr. </hi>vi. (1852) S. 108 and <hi type="italic">Zur Einleitung in die Psalmen</hi>. An academical programme, 1859. 4to.</note> <div eID="gen9075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9076" type="x-p"/> It is true sacrifice was offered in Gibeon, where the old tabernacle and the old altars (or at least the altar of burnt-offering) were, and also that after the removal of the ark to Zion both David (1Ch 21:29.) and Solomon (1Ki 3:4; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.2-2Chr.1.6">2Ch 1:2-6</reference>) worshipped and sacrificed in Gibeon. But it is self-evident sacrifices might have been offered where the ark was, and that even with greater right than in Gibeon; and since both David, upon its arrival (2Sa 6:17.), and Solomon after his accession (1Ki 3:15), offered sacrifices through the priests who were placed there, it is probable-and by a comparison of the Davidic Psalms not to be doubted-that there was a daily service, in conjunction with sacrifices, before the ark on Zion. <div eID="gen9076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9077" type="x-p"/> But, moreover, is it really the אהל in Zion which is meant here in v. 8 by the house of God? It is still maintained by renowned critics that the tabernacle pitched by David over the sacred ark is never called בית ה or היכל or משׁכן ה or מקדשׁ or קדשׁ. But why could it not have all these names? We will not appeal to the fact that the house of God at Shilo (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.9">1Sa 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.3">1Sa 3:3</reference>) is called בית and היכל ה, since it may be objected that it was really more of a temple than a tabernacle,<note placement="foot">Vid., C. H. Graf, <hi type="italic">Commentation de templo Silonensi ad illustrandum locum Jud</hi>. xviii. 30, 31, (1855, 4to.), in which he seeks to prove that the sanctuary in Shilo was a temple to Jahve that lasted until the dissolution of the kingdom of Israel.</note> although in the same book, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.22">1Sa 2:22</reference> it is called אהל מועד, and in connection with the other appellations the poetic colouring of the historical style of 1 Sam 1-3 is to be taken into consideration. Moreover, we put aside passages like <reference osisRef="Exod.23.19">Exo 23:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.26">Exo 34:26</reference>, since it may be said that the future Temple was present to the mind of the Lawgiver. But in <reference osisRef="Josh.6.24">Jos 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.20">2Sa 12:20</reference>, the sanctuary is called בית ה without being conceived of as a temple. Why then cannot the tabernacle, which David pitched for the ark of the covenant when removed to Zion (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.17">2Sa 6:17</reference>), be called בית ה? It is only when אהל and בּית are placed in opposition to one another that the latter has the notion of a dwelling built of more solid materials; but in itself <hi type="italic">beit</hi> (bêt) in Semitic is the generic term for housing of every kind whether it be made of wool, felt, and hair-cloth, or of earth, stone, and wood; consequently it is just as much a tent as a house (in the stricter sense of the word), whether the latter be a hut built of wood and clay or a palace.<note placement="foot">The Turkish Kamus says: “Arab. <hi type="italic">byt</hi> is a house (Turk. <hi type="italic">ew</hi>) in the signification of <hi type="italic">châne</hi> (Persic the same), whether it be made of hair, therefore a tent, or built of stone and tiles.” And further on: “<hi type="italic">Beit</hi> originally signified a place specially designed for persons to retire to at night from Arab. <hi type="italic">bâta</hi> he has passed the night, if it does not perhaps come from the בוא, Arab. <hi type="italic">bayya</hi>, which stands next to it in this passage, vid., <hi type="italic">Job</hi> at <reference osisRef="Job.29.15">Job 29:15</reference>-17]; but later on the meaning was extended and the special reference to the night time was lost.” Even at the present day the Beduin does not call his tent <hi type="italic">ahl</hi>, but always <hi type="italic">bêt</hi> and in fact <hi type="italic">bêt sha'r</hi> (בית שׂער), the modern expression for the older <hi type="italic">bêt wabar</hi> (hair-house).</note> <div eID="gen9077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9078" type="x-p"/> If a dwelling-house is frequently called אהל, then a tent that any one dwells in may the more naturally be called his בּית. And this we find is actually the case with the dwellings of the patriarchs, which, although they were not generally solid houses (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.17">Gen 33:17</reference>), are called בית (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.15">Gen 27:15</reference>). Moreover, היכל (from יכל = כּוּל to hold, <hi type="italic">capacem esse</hi>), although it signifies a palace does not necessarily signify one of stone, for the heavens are also called Jahve’s היכל, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>, and not necessarily one of gigantic proportions, for even the Holy of holies of Solomon’s Temple, and this <hi type="italic">par excellence</hi>, is called היכל, and once, 1Ki 6:3, היכל הבּית. Of the spaciousness and general character of the Davidic tabernacle we know indeed nothing: it certainly had its splendour, and was not so much a substitute for the original tabernacle, which according to the testimony of the chronicler remained in Gibeon, as a substitute for the Temple that was still to be built. But, however insignificant it may have been, Jahve had His throne there, and it was therefore the היבל of a great king, just as the wall-less place in the open field where God manifested Himself with His angels to the homeless Jacob was בּית אלהים (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.17">Gen 28:17</reference>). <div eID="gen9078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9079" type="x-p"/> Into this tabernacle of God, i.e., into its front court, will David enter (בּוא with <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13">Psa 66:13</reference>) this morning, there will he prostrate himself in worship, προσκυνεῖν (השׁתּחוה) reflexive of the <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> שׁחוה, Ges. §75, rem. 18), towards (אל as in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>, 1Ki 8:29, 1Ki 8:35, cf. ל <reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">Psa 99:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.9">Psa 99:9</reference>) Jahve’s היכל קדשׁ, i.e., the דּביר, the Holy of holies <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>, and that “in Thy fear,” i.e., in reverence before Thee (<hi type="italic">genit. objectivus</hi>). The going into the Temple which David purposes, leads his thoughts on to his way through life, and the special de'eesis, which only begins here, moulds itself accordingly: he prays for God’s gracious guidance as in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">Psa 86:11</reference>, and frequently. The direction of God, by which he wishes to be guided he calls צדקה. Such is the general expression for the determination of conduct by an ethical rule. The rule, acting in accordance with which, God is called <hi type="italic">par excellence</hi> צדיק, is the order of salvation which opens up the way of mercy to sinners. When God forgives those who walk in this way their sins, and stands near to bless and protect them, He shows Himself not less צדיק (just), than when He destroys those who despise Him, in the heat of His rejected love. By this righteousness, which accords with the counsel and order of mercy, David prays to be led למען שׁוררי, in order that the malicious desire of those who lie in wait for him may not be fulfilled, but put to shame, and that the honour of God may not be sullied by him. שׁורר is equivalent to משׁורר (Aquila ἐφοδεύων, Jerome <hi type="italic">insidiator</hi>) from the <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> שׁורר to fix one’s eyes sharply upon, especially of hostile observation. David further prays that God will make his way (i.e., the way in which a man must walk according to God’s will) even and straight before him, the prayer one, in order that he may walk therein without going astray and unimpeded. The adj. ישׂר signifies both the straightness of a line and the evenness of a surface. The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הישׁיר is יישׁיר in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.25">Pro 4:25</reference>, and accordingly the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> substitutes for the <hi type="italic">imper</hi>. הושׁר the corresponding form הישׁר, just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.2">Isa 45:2</reference> it removes the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> form אושׁר (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.8.17">Gen 8:17</reference> הוצא Keri היצא), without any grammatical, but certainly not without some traditional ground. כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.10">Psa 5:10</reference> is closely connected with למען שׁוררי: on account of my way-layers, for the following are their characteristics. אין is separated by בּפיהוּ (= בּפיו <reference osisRef="Ps.62.5">Psa 62:5</reference>) from נכונה the word it governs; this was the more easily possible as the usage of the language almost entirely lost sight of the fact that אין is the construct of אין, Ges. §152, 1. In his mouth is nothing that should stand firm, keep its ground, remain the same (cf. Job 42:7.). The singular suffix of בפיהו has a distributive meaning: <hi type="italic">in ore unuiscujusque eorum</hi>. Hence the <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. at once passes over into the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>.: קרבּם הוּות their inward part, i.e., that towards which it goes forth and in which it has its rise (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">Psa 49:12</reference>) is הוות corruption, from הוּה which comes from הוה = Arab. <hi type="italic">hawâ</hi>, to yawn, gape, χαίνειν, <hi type="italic">hiare</hi>, a yawning abyss and a gaping vacuum, and then, inasmuch as, starting from the primary idea of an empty space, the verbal significations <hi type="italic">libere ferri</hi> (especially from below upwards) and more particularly <hi type="italic">animo ad</hi> or <hi type="italic">in aliquid ferri</hi> are developed, it obtains the pathological sense of strong desire, passion, just as it does also the intellectual sense of a loose way of thinking proceeding from a self-willed tendency (vid., Fleischer on <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference>). In Hebrew the prevalent meaning of the word is corruption, <reference osisRef="Ps.57.2">Psa 57:2</reference>, which is a metaphor for the abyss, <hi type="italic">barathrum</hi>, (so far, but only so far Schultens on <reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">Pro 10:3</reference> is right), and proceeding from this meaning it denotes both that which is physically corruptible (<reference osisRef="Job.6.30">Job 6:30</reference>) and, as in the present passage and frequently, that which is corruptible from an ethical point of view. The meaning strong desire, in which הוּה looks as though it only differed from אוּה in one letter, occurs only in <reference osisRef="Ps.52.9">Psa 52:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">Pro 10:3</reference>; Mic 7:3. The substance of their inward part is that which is corruptible in every way, and their throat, as the organ of speech, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.7">Psa 115:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.149.6">Psa 149:6</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>, is (perhaps a figure connected with the primary meaning of הוות) a grave, which yawns like jaws, which open and snatch and swallow down whatever comes in their way. To this “they make smooth their tongue” is added as a circumstantial clause. Their throat is thus formed and adapted, while they make smooth their tongue (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pro 2:16</reference>), in order to conceal their real design beneath flattering language. From this meaning, החליק directly signifies to flatter in <reference osisRef="Ps.36.3">Psa 36:3</reference>; Pro 29:5. The last two lines of the strophe are formed according to the caesura schema. This schema is also continued in the concluding strophe.
entries.efd3aaa24bf459ffbe7893a6f73276cb8c755d26: <reference osisRef="Ps.5.10-Ps.5.12">Psa 5:10-12</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_5:11-13) The verb אשׁם or אשׁם unites in itself the three closely allied meanings of becoming guilty (e.g., <reference osisRef="Lev.5.19">Lev 5:19</reference>), of a feeling of guilt (Lev 5:4.), and of expiation (Psa 34:22.); just as the verbal adj. אשׁם also signifies both liable to punishment and expiating, and the substantive אשׁם both the guilt to be expiated and the expiation. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. האשׁים signifies to cause any one to render the expiation due to his fault, to make him do penance. As an exception God is here, in the midst of the Jehovic Psalms, called אלהים, perhaps not altogether unintentionally as being God the Judge. The מן of ממּעצותיהם (with <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> by the מן and a transition of the counter-tone <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> into <hi type="italic">Galgal</hi>, as in Hos 11:6 into <hi type="italic">Meajla</hi>, vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi> ii. 526) is certainly that of the cause in Hos 11:6, but here it is to be explained with Olsh. and Hitz. according to Sir. 14:2, Judith 11:6 (cf. Hos 10:6): may they fall from their own counsels, i.e., founder in the execution of them. Therefore מן in the sense of “down from, away,” a sense which the parallel הדּיחמו thrust them away (cf. דּחוּ from דּחה Ps 36:13), presupposes. The ב of בּרב is to be understood according to Joh 8:21, Joh 8:24 “ye shall die ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν." The multitude of their transgressions shall remain unforgiven and in this state God is to cast them into hades. The ground of this terrible prayer is set forth by כּי מרוּ בך. The tone of מרוּ, for a well-known reason (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.37.40">Psa 37:40</reference>; 64:11; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Psa 72:17</reference>) has retreated to the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. מרה, root מר, prop. to be or hold one’s self stiff towards any one, compare Arab. <hi type="italic">mârr , tmârr</hi>, to press and stiffen against one another in wrestling, Arab. <hi type="italic">mârâ , tmârâ</hi>, to struggle against anything, whether with outward or mental and moral opposition. Their obstinacy is not obstinacy against a man, but against God Himself; their sin is, therefore, Satanic and on that account unpardonable. All the prayers of this character are based upon the assumption expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.13">Psa 7:13</reference>, that those against whom they are directed do not wish for mercy. Accordingly their removal is prayed for. Their removal will make the <hi type="italic">ecclesia pressa</hi> free and therefore joyous. From this point of view the prayer in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.12">Psa 5:12</reference> is inspired by the prospect of the result of their removal. The <hi type="italic">futt</hi>. do not express a wish, but a consequence. The division of the verse is, however, incorrect. The rise of the first half of the verse closes with בך (the pausal form by <hi type="italic">Pazer</hi>), its fall is לעולם ירנּנוּ; then the rise begins anew in the second half, extending to בך which ought likewise to be pointed בך, and אהבי שׁמך is its fall. ותסך עלימו (from הסך <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of סכך <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">Psa 91:4</reference>) is awkward in this sequence of thoughts. Hupfeld and Hitzig render it: “they shall rejoice for ever whom Thou defendest;” but then it ought not only to be pointed ירנּנוּ, but the ו must also be removed, and yet there is nothing to characterise תסך עלימו as being virtually a subject. On the other hand it does not harmonise with the other consecutive futures. It must therefore, like יפּלוּ, be the optative: “And do Thou defend them, then shall those who love Thy name rejoice in Thee.” And then upon this this joy of those who love the name of Jahve (i.e., God in His revelation of Himself in redemption) Ps 69:37; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.132">Psa 119:132</reference>, is based by כּי־אתּה from a fact of universal experience which is the sum of all His historical self-attestations. עלימו is used instead of עליהם as a graver form of expression, just like הדּיחמו for הדּיחם as an indignant one. The form ויעלצוּ (Ges. §§63, 3) is chosen instead of the יעלצוּ found in <reference osisRef="Ps.25.2">Psa 25:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.4">Psa 68:4</reference>, in order to assist the rhythm. The <hi type="italic">futt</hi>. are continuative. תּעטרנּוּ, <hi type="italic">cinges eum</hi>, is not a contracted <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.25">1Sa 17:25</reference>, but <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.26">1Sa 23:26</reference>; here it is used like the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.8.6">Psa 8:6</reference> with a double accusative. The צנּה (from צנן Arab. <hi type="italic">tsân , med. Waw</hi>, Aethiop. צון to hedge round, guard) is a shield of a largest dimensions; larger than מגן   1Ki 10:16. (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.7">1Sa 17:7</reference>, where Goliath has his צנּה borne by a shield-bearer). כּצּנּה “like a shield” is equivalent to: as with a shield (Ges. §118, 3, rem.). The name of God, יהוה, is correctly drawn to the second member of the verse by the accentuation, in order to balance it with the first; and for this reason the first clause does not begin with כי־אתה יהוה here as it does elsewhere (Ps 4:9; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.8">Psa 12:8</reference>). רצון delight, goodwill, is also a synonym for the divine blessing in Deu 33:23.  <chapter eID="Ps.5"/> <div eID="gen9079" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 5.
David being grievously oppressed by the cruelty of his enemies, and apprehending still more mischief, earnestly beseeches God for help. And the more easily to obtain what he asks, after having, by the earnestness of his prayers, manifested the greatness of his grief, he first brings forward the intolerable malice of his enemies, showing how inconsistent it would be with the character of God, were they to be left unpunished. He next speaks of his own faith and patience, and even comfort; having no doubt whatever of a happy issue. Finally, he concludes, that when he shall be delivered, the benefits resulting from his deliverance would not be limited to himself, but would extend to all the godly.
To the chief musician upon Nehiloth. A psalm of David.
Some translate the Hebrew word Nehiloth, heritages, and others, armies. The former assign this reason for their opinion, that David prayed for the welfare of the twelve tribes, whom he calls heritages.
“Qu’il appelle Heritages.” — Fr.
The latter assert in support of their view, that being besieged by a vast multitude of men, he betook himself to God for succor; and, according to this sense, the word upon will signify against. But not approving of the conjectures of many who speak upon these inscriptions of The Psalms as if they were riddles,
“Mais pource que je n’approuve point ce que devinent plusieurs parlans comme par enigmes sur ces inscriptions des Pseaumes.” — Fr.
I adopt the opinion of those who hold that it was either a musical instrument or a tune; but of what particular kind I consider it of little importance to ascertain.
Psalm 5:1-2
1. Give ear unto my words, O Jehovah; attend to my speech. 2. Hearken to the voice of my cry, my King and my God: for unto thee will I pray.
 
I presume not positively to determine whether David, in this psalm, bewails the wrongs which he suffered from his enemies at some particular time, or whether he complains generally of the various persecutions with which, for a long time, he was harassed under Saul. Some of the Jewish commentators apply the psalm even to Absalom; because, by the bloody and deceitful man, they think Doeg and Ahithophel are pointed out. To me, however, it appears more probable, that when David, after the death of Saul, had got peaceable possession of the kingdoms he committed to writing the prayers which he had meditated in his afflictions and dangers. But to come to the words:— First, he expresses one thing in three different ways; and this repetition denotes the strength of his affection, and his long perseverance in prayer. For he was not so fond of many words as to employ different forms of expression, which had no meaning; but being deeply engaged in prayer, he represented, by these various expressions, the variety of his complaints.
“Il a aussi represente et exprime ses gemissemens qui estoyent en grand nombre et de beaucoup de sortes.” — Fr.
It therefore signifies, that he prayed neither coldly nor only in few words; but that, according as the vehemence of his grief urged him, he was earnest in bewailing his calamities before God; and that since it did not immediately appear what would be their issue, he persevered in repeating the same complaints. Again, he does not expressly state what he desires to ask from God:
“Ce qu’il vent requerir a Dieu.” —Fr.
but there is a greater force in this kind of suppression, than if he had spoken distinctly. By not uttering the desires of his heart, he shows more emphatically that his inward feelings, which he brought with him before God, were such that language was insufficient to express them. Again, the word cry, which signifies a loud and sonorous utterance of the voice, serves to mark the earnestness of his desire. David did not cry out as it were into the ears of one who was deaf; but the vehemence of his grief and his inward anguish, burst forth into this cry. The verb הגהhagah, from which the noun הגיג, hagig, speech, which the prophet here uses, is derived, means both to speak distinctly, and to whisper or to mutter. But the second sense seems better suited to this passage.
Bishop Horne beautifully renders the word, “dove-like mournings,” and Bishop Horsley, “sighing.” “The word,” says Hammond, “regularly signifies sighing or cry, not a loud, sonorous voice, but such as complaints are made in.”
After David has said in general, that God hears his words, he seems, immediately after, for the purpose of being more specific, to divide them into two kinds, calling the one obscure or indistinct moanings, and the other loud crying.
“Il semble que puis apres, pour mieux specifier, it en met deux sortes appelant les unes Complaintes obscures, et les autres Cri.” — Fr.
By the first he means a confused muttering, such as is described in the Song of Hezekiah, when sorrow hindered him from speaking distinctly, and making his voice to be heard. “Like a crane, or a swallow, so did I chatter; I did mourn as a dove,” (Isaiah 38:14.)
“Quand la douleur l’empesche de parler distinctement et faire entendre sa voix.” — Fr.
If, then, at any time we are either backward to pray, or our devout affections begin to lose their fervor, we must here seek for arguments to quicken and urge us forward. And as by calling God his King and his God, he intended to stir up himself to entertain more lively and favorable hopes with respect to the issue of his afflictions, let us learn to apply these titles to a similar use, namely, for the purpose of making ourselves more familiar with God. At the close, he testifies that he does not sullenly gnaw the bit, as unbelievers are accustomed to do; but directs his groaning to God: for they who, disregarding God, either fret inwardly or utter their complaints to men, are not worthy of being regarded by him. Some translate the last clause thus, When I pray to thee; but to me it seems rather to be the reason which David assigns for what he had said immediately before, and that his purpose is, to encourage himself to trust in God, by assuming this as a general principle that whoever call upon God in their calamities never meet with a repulse from him.
Psalm 5:3
3. O that thou wouldst hear my voice in the morning; O Jehovah, in the morning will I direct unto thee, and I will keep watch.

PSAL, V. To the chief musician upon Nehiloth This is no where else used in Scripture. It is generally and probably thought to be a term belonging to Musick, and to signify either some kind of tune: or rather an Instrument, and particularly a wind-instrument, as Neginoth in the title of the last Psalm signified stringed Instruments.
                     , A psalm of David This Psalm supposeth David to be in some great distress or trouble, either from Saul, or from Absalom, or some of their Courtiers..
